name: Bar Chart
description: Compares discrete categories using the length of rectangular bars. One of the most versatile and universally understood chart types.
use_cases: Comparing values across categories (sales by region, votes by party)
Showing rankings or league tables
Tracking a single metric across time periods
not_use_cases: Showing continuous trends over time (use a line chart)
Displaying part-to-whole relationships (use a pie or stacked bar)
More than ~20 categories — it becomes unreadable

name: Bubble Chart
description: A scatter plot where a third variable is encoded as the area of each circle, allowing three dimensions of data to be shown at once.
use_cases: Comparing entities across three variables simultaneously (e.g. country GDP, population, life expectancy)
Showing relative size alongside position
Making data feel more engaging and visual
not_use_cases: Precise value comparison — humans are poor at judging circle area
More than ~50 data points — overlapping becomes unreadable
When the third variable isn't meaningful (use scatter instead)

name: Lollipop Chart
description: A cleaner alternative to bar charts using a dot on a thin stem to encode a single numeric value per category.
use_cases: Ranking countries by life expectancy without the visual weight of a full bar chart
Comparing performance metrics for a large number of items where bars would feel cluttered
Displaying sparse data where the dot position is more important than bar area
not_use_cases: When showing part-to-whole composition — segments cannot be added to lollipop stems
When the audience expects conventional bar charts in a formal report context
When values are very close together and the dot difference is imperceptible

name: Dot Plot
description: Individual data points are plotted as dots along an axis, making distribution and individual values easy to read.
use_cases: Comparing average life expectancy across countries while showing individual country dots
Displaying test scores for each student in a class to see spread and outliers
Ranking products by rating with each dot representing a review score
not_use_cases: When the dataset is so large that dots overlap and obscure the distribution — use beeswarm or histogram
When showing change over time across many periods — use a line chart
When part-to-whole relationships are more important than individual comparisons

name: Line Chart
description: Connects data points with a continuous line to show how a value changes over time or across a continuous variable.
use_cases: Showing how a value changes over time (stock price, temperature, revenue)
Comparing trends across multiple series
Highlighting a rate of change or inflection point
not_use_cases: Comparing discrete, unrelated categories (use a bar chart)
Data with fewer than 3 points — a line implies continuous change
Showing part-to-whole composition

name: Area Chart
description: A line chart where the area beneath the line is filled, emphasising the volume or magnitude of change over time.
use_cases: Showing cumulative totals over time
Emphasising the scale of change, not just the direction
Stacked area charts for part-to-whole over time
not_use_cases: Multiple overlapping series — filled areas obscure each other
When the baseline isn't zero — can be visually misleading
Communicating precise values (use a line chart)

name: Step Chart
description: A line chart variant where values change in discrete steps rather than smooth interpolation, ideal for data that holds a value until it changes.
use_cases: Showing a central bank's interest rate held flat then raised at policy meetings
Visualizing software version releases that stay current until the next version ships
Displaying a utility's tiered pricing that changes at discrete consumption thresholds
not_use_cases: When values change continuously and interpolation between points is meaningful
When showing smooth trends where the staircase shape would imply false precision
When the data is categorical rather than a true held value over time

name: Scatter Plot
description: Plots individual data points on two axes to reveal correlations, clusters, and outliers between two continuous variables.
use_cases: Exploring the relationship between two numeric variables
Identifying clusters or outliers in a dataset
Showing the spread of a population
not_use_cases: Categorical data — both axes should be continuous
Very small datasets where patterns can't emerge
Communicating to general audiences without guidance

name: Pie Chart
description: A circular chart divided into slices to show how a whole is broken into parts. Best when there are few, clearly differentiated slices.
use_cases: Showing how a total is divided into a small number of parts (2–5)
Communicating a dominant share (e.g. one category > 50%)
Simple, audience-friendly breakdowns
not_use_cases: More than 5–6 slices — comparison becomes impossible
Values that are close to each other in size
When the exact percentages matter more than the visual impression

name: Heatmap
description: Uses colour intensity on a grid to encode a numeric value, making it easy to spot patterns across two categorical dimensions.
use_cases: Showing activity patterns over time (GitHub contribution graph, weekly traffic by hour)
Comparing two categorical dimensions on a third numeric value
Identifying anomalies or clusters in a large dataset
not_use_cases: Audiences who are colour-blind without careful palette choice
When precise values are needed (colour is imprecise)
Data with many unique values in the grid — cells become tiny

name: Treemap
description: Uses nested rectangles to represent hierarchical data, where the area of each rectangle encodes a numeric value.
use_cases: Showing the relative size of many parts within a whole (market share, file sizes, budget breakdown)
Displaying hierarchical data (categories and subcategories)
When you have too many parts for a pie chart
not_use_cases: Showing change over time
When precise comparison is needed — area is hard to judge
Deeply nested hierarchies with many levels

name: Histogram
description: Shows the distribution of a single continuous variable by grouping values into bins and displaying the frequency of each bin as a bar.
use_cases: Showing how values are distributed across a range (age distribution, response times, test scores)
Identifying skew, outliers, or bimodal distributions
Comparing distributions across groups
not_use_cases: Categorical data (use a bar chart)
Very small datasets where bins are nearly empty
When exact values matter more than the overall shape

name: Box Plot
description: Summarises a distribution using five statistics — minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum — making it easy to compare spread and skew across groups.
use_cases: Comparing distributions across multiple groups or categories
Highlighting outliers in the data
Summarising large datasets compactly
not_use_cases: General audiences unfamiliar with statistics
Small datasets where a dot plot would show actual values
When the shape of the distribution matters (use a violin or histogram)

name: Sankey Diagram
description: Shows flows between nodes, where the width of each flow is proportional to the quantity it represents. Great for visualising how a total is distributed through stages.
use_cases: Showing how a budget or energy is allocated across departments or uses
Visualising user journeys or conversion funnels
Tracking the flow of materials, money, or people through a system
not_use_cases: Cyclic flows — Sankeys are directional
Simple comparisons that a bar chart would handle more clearly
Very large numbers of nodes — becomes visually overwhelming

name: Chord Diagram
description: Shows relationships and flows between entities arranged around a circle, with arcs connecting them proportionally to the flow volume.
use_cases: Showing bilateral flows between a fixed set of entities (trade between countries, migrations)
Visualising a relationship matrix in a compelling way
When the symmetry and proportionality of relationships matter
not_use_cases: More than ~10 entities — becomes very cluttered
One-directional flows (use a Sankey diagram)
General audiences — requires explanation

name: Funnel Chart
description: Shows progressive reduction of a value through sequential stages, commonly used for conversion analysis.
use_cases: Tracking conversion rates through a sales or marketing pipeline
Showing drop-off at each stage of a user journey
Highlighting where the biggest losses occur in a process
not_use_cases: Data without a clear sequential order
When stages are not subsets of the previous stage
Showing multiple parallel funnels (gets very busy)

name: Radar Chart
description: Plots multiple variables on axes radiating from a central point, with the enclosed area showing the overall profile of an entity.
use_cases: Comparing an entity's performance across multiple dimensions (e.g. a product's attributes)
Showing strength and weakness profiles
Overlaying two or three entities to compare overall shapes
not_use_cases: More than 3 entities — overlapping polygons become unreadable
When precise values matter (radial scales are hard to read)
Data where some axes have very different scales or directions

name: Waffle Chart
description: A grid of equal-sized cells where filled cells represent a proportion of the whole — a more readable alternative to a pie chart.
use_cases: Communicating a percentage to a general audience in an intuitive way
Showing a single key statistic (e.g. 1 in 3 people...)
Making a data story more visual and engaging
not_use_cases: More than 3–4 categories
Values that don't round to a clean percentage
When you need spatial precision

name: Grouped Bar Chart
description: Displays multiple bar series side by side to compare values across categories and groups simultaneously.
use_cases: Comparing quarterly revenue across multiple product lines for a single year
Showing test scores by subject for different student cohorts
Contrasting survey responses across demographic groups for each question
not_use_cases: When you have more than 4-5 groups, causing bars to become too narrow to read
When showing part-to-whole relationships within a total — use stacked bar instead
When tracking continuous change over time — use a line chart instead

name: Stacked Bar Chart
description: Bars are divided into coloured segments stacked on top of each other to show part-to-whole relationships across categories.
use_cases: Showing how each department's budget contributes to total company spend across years
Displaying the breakdown of energy sources for each country
Visualizing survey response distributions (agree/neutral/disagree) per question
not_use_cases: When comparing individual segment sizes across bars — interior segments lack a common baseline
When you have many small segments that become hard to distinguish
When precise comparisons of sub-categories matter more than totals — use grouped bar instead

name: 100% Stacked Bar Chart
description: Each bar is normalised to 100% so segments show proportional composition rather than absolute values.
use_cases: Comparing the proportion of market share held by competitors across different regions
Showing the relative breakdown of age groups in a population over several decades
Displaying survey sentiment ratios across multiple product categories
not_use_cases: When absolute magnitudes are important alongside proportions — totals are hidden
When there are only two categories — a single line chart or diverging bar is cleaner
When the number of segments per bar exceeds 5-6, making proportions hard to compare

name: Dumbbell Chart
description: Shows the difference between two values for each category using dots connected by a horizontal or vertical line.
use_cases: Showing the gap in male vs female salaries across job categories
Comparing a country's performance in two different years on a single metric
Visualizing the difference between a target and actual value for each item
not_use_cases: When comparing more than two data points per category — use slope chart or parallel coordinates instead
When the two endpoints have no meaningful relationship to each other
When showing cumulative or part-to-whole data

name: Slope Chart
description: Connects two or more time points with lines to highlight rank changes or value shifts between periods.
use_cases: Showing how country rankings shifted between two Olympic games
Comparing employee satisfaction scores before and after a workplace policy change
Visualizing the change in market share for several companies between two years
not_use_cases: When there are more than 3-4 time points — a line chart handles multiple periods better
When too many lines cross and create visual clutter with many categories
When precise values are needed rather than general directional change

name: Donut Chart
description: A pie chart with a hollow centre, often used to display a key metric or label in the empty space.
use_cases: Showing market share breakdown while displaying total revenue in the centre hole
Displaying a completion percentage with the remaining portion as context
Presenting survey response distribution with a summary stat in the middle
not_use_cases: When precise comparisons between many slices are needed — angles are hard to judge
When there are more than 5-6 categories, making the arcs too thin to distinguish
When showing change over time — use a line or area chart instead

name: Sunburst Chart
description: A radial, multi-level pie chart that displays hierarchical data as nested rings radiating outward.
use_cases: Showing the hierarchical breakdown of a company's organisational budget by department and team
Visualizing file system structure where size encodes storage usage at each folder level
Displaying a taxonomy of species from kingdom down to genus as nested segments
not_use_cases: When precise comparisons between segments at the same level are needed — arc area is hard to judge
When the hierarchy is shallow (one or two levels) — a treemap or pie chart is simpler
When data has no meaningful hierarchical structure

name: Waterfall Chart
description: Shows how an initial value increases or decreases through a series of intermediate positive and negative contributions.
use_cases: Breaking down a company's net income by showing revenue minus each expense category
Visualizing how starting headcount changes through hires, departures, and transfers to reach end count
Explaining the change in account balance through individual debit and credit transactions
not_use_cases: When there is no meaningful starting total that subsequent values modify
When changes are all in the same direction — a simple bar chart is clearer
When showing continuous change over many time steps — a line chart is more appropriate

name: Gantt Chart
description: Horizontal bars on a timeline axis show the start, end, and duration of tasks or events in a project schedule.
use_cases: Planning a product launch by mapping each development phase with start and end dates
Scheduling construction project tasks to identify overlaps and critical path dependencies
Visualizing an event agenda with overlapping sessions across multiple tracks
not_use_cases: When tasks have no meaningful temporal duration or sequence
When the focus is on data trends or distributions rather than scheduling
When the number of tasks is very small and a simple list communicates more clearly

name: Bullet Chart
description: A compact bar chart that compares a primary measure against a target and qualitative performance ranges in a single bar.
use_cases: Displaying a salesperson's actual revenue vs their monthly quota with a performance band
Showing a project's current completion percentage against a target with risk zones
Comparing a product's customer satisfaction score against a benchmark within a dashboard
not_use_cases: When there is no meaningful target or benchmark to compare the primary value against
When the qualitative ranges (poor/satisfactory/good) are not defined or meaningful
When multiple values per category need to be compared — use a grouped bar instead

name: Strip Plot
description: All individual data points for one or more categories are plotted as dots along a single axis, often with jitter.
use_cases: Showing the distribution of exam scores across multiple school classes simultaneously
Displaying all individual response times for an API endpoint to spot outliers
Comparing salary distributions across departments when sample sizes are small
not_use_cases: When the dataset is very large and dots become an unreadable mass — use violin or density plot
When summary statistics are more important than individual point visibility
When showing change over time rather than distributional spread

name: Beeswarm Plot
description: Data points are arranged along an axis without overlap, like a swarm of bees, to show distribution and individual values.
use_cases: Displaying the distribution of salaries across job levels without dot overlap obscuring density
Showing individual country values on a human development index for each continent
Visualizing performance scores for athletes in each event category
not_use_cases: When sample sizes are extremely large and the swarm becomes too wide to fit the layout
When the key message is a summary statistic rather than individual points — use box plot
When categories have very different sample sizes, making comparisons misleading

name: Violin Plot
description: Combines a box plot with a kernel density estimate to show the full distribution shape of a numeric variable.
use_cases: Comparing the distribution of customer waiting times across multiple service centres
Showing how the distribution of gene expression levels differs between treatment groups
Visualizing the spread and skewness of daily temperatures across different climate zones
not_use_cases: When sample sizes are very small and the density estimate is unreliable and misleading
When precise individual data points are needed — use beeswarm or strip plot instead
When the audience is unfamiliar with statistical charts and needs a simpler summary

name: Density Plot
description: A smoothed continuous curve estimated from data to show the probability distribution of a numeric variable.
use_cases: Comparing the income distribution shapes of two countries on the same axis
Showing the distribution of model prediction errors to check for normality
Overlapping multiple groups' age distributions to see where they differ
not_use_cases: When the exact count of values in bins matters — use a histogram for that
When sample sizes are too small to produce a reliable density estimate
When the variable is categorical or discrete rather than continuous

name: Ridge Plot
description: Multiple overlapping density curves stacked vertically to compare distributions across many groups compactly.
use_cases: Comparing the distribution of temperatures by month across a full year in a compact layout
Showing how listening time distributions differ across music genres in a streaming dataset
Visualizing the shift in customer age distributions across multiple product categories
not_use_cases: When you have only two or three groups — overlapping density plots or a violin plot suffice
When precise values matter and the overlap between curves causes confusion
When the distributions are nearly identical, making the chart uninformative

name: Parallel Coordinates Plot
description: Multiple vertical axes represent different variables, with each data item drawn as a line connecting its values across axes.
use_cases: Exploring how car models differ across horsepower, weight, fuel economy, and price simultaneously
Identifying clusters of patients with similar profiles across multiple clinical measurements
Comparing candidate job applications across multiple weighted criteria at once
not_use_cases: When there are only two or three variables — a scatter plot or scatter matrix is cleaner
When the dataset is very large and lines create an unreadable hairball of crossings
When a non-technical audience needs to quickly extract a simple insight

name: Stacked Area Chart
description: Area layers stacked on top of each other show how multiple series contribute to a changing total over time.
use_cases: Showing how different energy sources contribute to total electricity generation over decades
Visualizing cumulative user sign-ups by acquisition channel over a product's lifetime
Displaying the changing composition of a portfolio's asset classes through market cycles
not_use_cases: When comparing individual series values precisely — interior layers have no common baseline
When series frequently cross each other, making stacking misleading
When there are many series with similar magnitudes causing indistinguishable layers

name: Streamgraph
description: A flowing, organic stacked area chart centred on a baseline, emphasising the relative rise and fall of categories over time.
use_cases: Showing the rise and fall of music genre popularity over several decades
Visualizing seasonal fluctuations in topic volumes across a news archive
Displaying the evolving dominance of programming languages in open-source repositories over time
not_use_cases: When precise values or exact comparisons between categories are required
When there are only two or three categories — a simple stacked area chart suffices
When data has no meaningful temporal flow or ordering

name: Connected Scatter Plot
description: Scatter plot points connected by lines in temporal or sequential order to show a path through two-dimensional space.
use_cases: Tracing a country's GDP vs life expectancy trajectory over several decades
Showing how a runner's heart rate and speed relate across the stages of a race
Visualizing the path of a stock's price and trading volume relationship through time
not_use_cases: When temporal order or sequential path is not meaningful — use a plain scatter plot
When there are many overlapping paths that create a confusing tangle of lines
When the relationship between the two variables is more important than the sequence

name: Bump Chart
description: Shows how the rank ordering of items changes over multiple time periods using smoothly curved lines.
use_cases: Tracking how Formula 1 teams move up and down the constructor standings throughout a season
Showing how countries' global competitiveness rankings shift year over year
Visualizing chart positions of music albums across multiple weekly charts
not_use_cases: When absolute values are more important than relative rank positions
When there are only two time points — a slope chart is simpler and clearer
When the number of ranked items is very large, making lines indistinguishable

name: Span Chart
description: Horizontal bars represent a range between a minimum and maximum value for each category, highlighting spread or duration.
use_cases: Displaying the temperature range (high and low) for each month in a city
Showing the salary band (minimum to maximum) for each job level at a company
Visualizing the confidence interval or margin of error for each survey question response
not_use_cases: When values have no meaningful minimum-maximum or start-end range structure
When part-to-whole composition is the message — use a stacked bar instead
When showing project task schedules — use a Gantt chart with proper temporal context

name: Calendar Heatmap
description: A grid laid out as a calendar where each day cell is colour-coded by a numeric value to reveal temporal patterns.
use_cases: Showing daily step counts over a year to reveal exercise patterns and streaks
Displaying daily sales revenue on a calendar to identify seasonal and weekday patterns
Visualizing commit frequency in a code repository across the year like GitHub's profile chart
not_use_cases: When data is not naturally structured by calendar day or has irregular time intervals
When precise value comparisons matter more than pattern detection — colour encoding limits precision
When the time range is very short and a simple bar or line chart shows more detail

name: Network Graph
description: Nodes and edges diagram showing relationships or connections between entities in a network or graph structure.
use_cases: Mapping social connections between users to identify communities and influencers
Visualizing dependencies between software packages in a codebase
Showing citation networks between academic papers to find influential research
not_use_cases: When relationships are purely hierarchical — use a tree diagram or sunburst instead
When the network is very dense and all nodes are connected, producing an unreadable hairball
When the goal is to show magnitudes or distributions rather than connections

name: Word Cloud
description: Words are sized proportionally to their frequency or importance and arranged in a cloud layout for quick thematic scanning.
use_cases: Giving a quick visual overview of the most common terms in customer survey feedback
Displaying trending hashtags on social media sized by mention volume
Summarizing the key themes from a politician's speech corpus at a glance
not_use_cases: When precise comparison of word frequencies is needed — a bar chart ranks terms more accurately
When the layout is arbitrary and similar-sized words appear far apart, implying false differences
When detailed analysis or filtering of text data is required beyond a visual impression

name: Pictogram
description: Uses repeated icons or symbols where each unit represents a fixed count, making quantities tangible and human-scale.
use_cases: Showing that 1 in 8 women will be diagnosed with breast cancer using a grid of figure icons
Communicating refugee population figures using people icons where each represents 1,000 people
Displaying survey results where icons replace abstract bar lengths for a general audience
not_use_cases: When precise numeric comparison across many categories is required
When the dataset involves non-integer or highly fractional values that icons cannot cleanly represent
When working in a context requiring dense data presentation without extra visual space

name: Proportional Symbol Map
description: A map where symbols, typically circles, are scaled to represent the magnitude of a variable at each geographic location.
use_cases: Showing earthquake magnitudes as scaled circles plotted on a world map
Displaying city population sizes using proportionally sized bubbles across a country map
Visualizing trade volume between ports with circle size encoding tonnage
not_use_cases: When geographic boundaries and regional rates matter more than point magnitudes — use choropleth
When symbols overlap heavily in dense regions and obscure each other
When the data has no meaningful geographic location component

name: Choropleth Map
description: Geographic regions are filled with colours representing a data variable, showing spatial patterns across boundaries.
use_cases: Showing vaccination rates across counties in a country using a colour scale from low to high
Displaying GDP per capita for each country in the world with a diverging colour scheme
Visualizing election results by constituency coloured by winning party
not_use_cases: When large but sparsely populated regions visually dominate despite low values
When the variable being mapped is a raw count rather than a normalised rate — large regions inflate perception
When precise local point-level data matters more than regional aggregates — use a symbol map

name: Marimekko Chart
description: A two-dimensional stacked bar chart where both bar width and segment height encode separate variables for a full market view.
use_cases: Showing both market segment size and each company's share within each segment simultaneously
Visualizing survey responses where bar width represents group sample size and height encodes answer proportions
Displaying product category revenue share alongside overall category market size
not_use_cases: When there are many categories making small segments too narrow to label or read
When only one dimension of data needs to be shown — use a standard stacked bar chart
When the audience is unfamiliar with reading two simultaneous encodings in a single chart

name: Error Bar Chart
description: Bars or points with attached lines showing the uncertainty, variability, or confidence interval around a central estimate.
use_cases: Displaying mean test scores with 95% confidence intervals for each teaching method being compared
Showing average monthly rainfall with standard deviation bars across cities
Presenting experimental results with error margins for each experimental condition
not_use_cases: When sample sizes are so large that confidence intervals are trivially small and invisible
When individual data points matter more than aggregated uncertainty — use beeswarm or strip plot
When a non-statistical audience will misinterpret error bars as min-max ranges

name: Candlestick Chart
description: Financial chart showing open, high, low, and close prices for each time period as coloured rectangular candles with wicks.
use_cases: Analysing daily price movements of a stock over three months to identify trading patterns
Displaying cryptocurrency price volatility over a selected time period for traders
Comparing the opening and closing price ranges of commodities across trading sessions
not_use_cases: When the data does not have a natural open/high/low/close structure
When a non-financial audience unfamiliar with candlestick conventions is viewing the chart
When a simple closing price trend line is sufficient — use a line chart for clarity

name: Gauge Chart
description: A semicircular or arc-shaped dial indicating a single value within a defined range, like a speedometer.
use_cases: Displaying a server's current CPU utilisation percentage on an operations dashboard
Showing a customer satisfaction NPS score relative to a target range on a business scorecard
Communicating a sales team's progress toward a quarterly target as a single clear metric
not_use_cases: When comparing multiple metrics simultaneously — multiple gauges waste space inefficiently
When showing change over time — a line chart or sparkline communicates trends far better
When the precise numeric value is more important than the visual impression of the level

name: Sparkline
description: A tiny, word-sized inline chart embedded in text or tables to show a trend without axes or labels.
use_cases: Embedding a 7-day price trend next to each stock ticker in a financial data table
Showing monthly revenue trends inline in a dashboard summary row for each product
Displaying heart rate variation over a workout session in a compact wearable app interface
not_use_cases: When precise values or labelled axes are required to interpret the chart correctly
When the trend spans very few data points and a simple up/down arrow communicates the same thing
When the chart will be displayed in isolation rather than as part of a larger data-dense context

name: Data Table
description: Organises data into labelled rows and columns to enable precise lookup and side-by-side comparison across multiple variables simultaneously.
use_cases: Comparing exact numeric values across multiple categories and metrics at once
Presenting audience or segment profiles side-by-side with a benchmark column
Showing mixed data types (percentages, counts, indices) that don't fit a single chart scale
not_use_cases: Communicating a single clear trend — a chart conveys the pattern far faster than scanning rows
Large datasets with many rows — readers lose the thread; consider a heatmap or chart instead
When the relationship between two variables is the story — use a scatter plot or line chart
